newsitem.title: YEMEN: FEATURE-Yemen pursues democracy balancing act.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Yemen pursues democracy balancing act.

text.p: Yemeni President Ali Abdullah Saleh, a former military officer, is brandishing a strange weapon these days to keep his opponents at bay in a land with a history of coups, assassinations and tribal feuds -- democracy.
Saleh's ruling General People's Congress (GPC) has swept through united Yemen's first parliamentary elections since a 1994 civil war, capturing 187 seats in the 301-member chamber.
The widely expected victory last month enables Saleh to tighten his grip on power and press ahead with sensitive economic reforms, Western diplomats and Yemeni analysts said.

But in Yemen, an impoverished land in a region where politics most often amounts to decree by kings and emirs, weaving democracy together can be just as daunting as settling tribal feuds that sometimes spread from village to palace.
Yemeni democracy, the analysts said, is walking a tightrope between giving the people a louder voice and taming the government's opponents.
"Politics in Yemen is just like its tribal society. One side is manipulated against the other by the leader," said a Western analyst.
"There is a debate in society. But real democracy will come when the president would be prepared to leave power peacefully."
ELECTIONS GIVE PRESIDENT POLITICAL AMMUNITION
That scenario does not seem likely any time soon now that the GPC has gained political ammunition in polls described by election observers as a step forward for Yemen's fledgling democracy.

Saleh came to power in North Yemen in 1978 after two of his predecessors were assassinated and has since mastered the art of co-opting everyone from his ambitious Islamist junior partners in government to feminists, analysts said.
"He plays the game very skilfully. Saleh uses his network of security, military and tribesmen to follow everything that is going on hour by hour," said the Western analyst.
"When small tribes are in a dispute, he lets people kill each other. But when there is a problem between important tribes, he arbitrates and sends his representatives," he added.

The volatility of Yemen's tribes and sub-tribes was underscored by the election's other tally -- 22 people died in violence in the campaign and polling period that officials said was linked to family or tribal disputes, not politics.

Yet the polls have helped Saleh project an image abroad of a functioning democracy -- necessary to convince foreign investors that it is safe to do business in Yemen, a small independent oil producer with annual per capita income of $280, analysts said.
POLITICAL DIVISIONS LINGER BETWEEN NORTH AND SOUTH
Election observers said the polls were relatively free and fair aside from a few irregularities. But encouraging words from election monitors will not make Saleh's task any easier.

Lingering mistrust between the Sanaa government and southern opposition figures tainted the elections and there is no sign that the president's southern opponents intend to bless Yemen's democratic experiment.

The main opposition Yemen Socialist Party (YSP), some of whose leaders launched the secessionist bid that triggered the civil war, and three others boycotted the election to protest alleged irregularities.
Officials have denied opposition allegations that the government used military and security personnel to fix the voter registration process.
"As long as the YSP stays out of the political process, Yemen's democracy will be flawed. Democracy will be stagnant," said a Western diplomat.
TENSIONS MOUNT WITHIN OUTGOING COALITION
Even the GPC's Islamist junior coalition partner, the Islah Party, is growing increasingly suspicious of the ruling party, accusing it of tampering with the elections.
Tensions between the GPC and Islah have been mounting, underscoring the sensitivity of Saleh's political balancing act.
The Islah won 53 seats, independents took 54 and two opposition parties captured a total of five seats in the elections.
Yemen is the only country in the Arabian peninsula with political parties, opposition newspapers and activist Islamist participation in government.
But Western diplomats said power ultimately lies with Saleh, appointed ministers and military and security forces loyal to the GPC. They describe the parliament as a pressure group.
And some Yemeni analysts warn that advancing democracy will require a lot more than symbols of horses, candles and camels on ballot slips to help the illiterate vote.

"Democracy exists in Yemen because it works for the interests of a few leaders. Democracy makes having a military coup more difficult. It will take another 10 to 15 years for democracy to have legs," said one.
In the meantime, Saleh will have to convince Yemenis that the vote, not the AK-47 assault rifle carried by many men -- will determine their future.
